items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S280

SPONSOR: BENJAMIN
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the administrative code of the city of New York, the
emergency tenant protection act of nineteen seventy-four, the emergency
housing rent control law and the civil practice law and rules, in
relation to the statute of limitations on rent overcharges for regulated
units; in relation to requiring owners to keep rent records for six
years; and in relation to deregulated units as a result of overcharges

 
PURPOSE:

This bill increases the statute of limitations and lookback window for
rent overcharges in rent regulated units from four years to six years.
The bill allows that owners or landlords can be penalized for rent over-
charges even when fraud or illegality is not found.  Additionally, a
certificate of eviction can be revoked if the certificate was granted as
a result of rent overcharges, regardless of whether there was fraud or
illegality. This bill returns units deregulated as a result of rent
overcharges to rent stabilization and authorizes penalties for rent
overcharges.

Penalties for rent such overcharges remain the same as before, but the
ability to levy them is broadened. In the case of willful overcharge,
the landlord shall pay the tenant three times the overcharge. If the
overcharge is not found to be willful, the penalty due the tenant will
be the amount of the overcharge plus interest. If the action is
commenced by the state, the tenant will be due one-third of such recov-
ered monies.

In the event a unit is deregulated as a result of overcharges, the unit
will be returned to rent stabilization within six months. If the owner
or landlord fails to register the unit as rent stabilized, DHCR will
impose a penalty of the amount of the overcharge plus interest. For each
year the owner/ landlord fails to register the unit, DHCR will impose an
penalty of at least $2000 but not more than $10000

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

§ 1 amends subdivisions a and g of section 26-516 of the administrative
code of the city of New York, subdivision a as amended by chapter 116 of
the laws of 1997 to extend the period for which rents can be examined
for overcharges from the period of four years to a period of six years
prior to filing of a complaint by a tenant.

§ 2 amends subdivision b and subparagraph (g) of paragraph 1 of subdivi-
sion g of section 26-405 of the administrative code of the city of New
York, subparagraph (g) of paragraph 1 of subdivision g as amended by
section 31 of part A of chapter 20 of the laws of 2015 to extend the
cause for finding a penalty for rent overcharges to include cases where
no illegality or fraud is proven. In subparagraph (g), a typographical
error in the statute is corrected.

§ 3 adds a new subdivision c to section 26-504.2 of the administrative
code of the city of New York extends the period of examination for rent
overcharges to be consistent with the provisions in § 1 of this act.

§ 4 adds a new section 26-504.4 to the administrative code of the city
of New York. This new section provides that in the event a rental unit
had been moved out of regulation by having a rent overcharge, that unit
will return to regulated status and sets penalties for failure to
comply.

§ 5 amends paragraph 1 of subdivision a of section 12 of section 4 of
chapter 576 of the laws of 1974, constituting the emergency tenant
protection act of nineteen seventy-four, as amended by chapter 403 of
the laws of 1983, the opening paragraph and clause (i) of subparagraph
(b) as amended by chapter 116 of the laws of 1997 to the effect that it
increases the period for examination for a rental overcharge to six
years from four or two years, dependent upon the circumstances.

§ 6 amends paragraph 8 of subdivision a of section 12 of section 4 of
chapter 576 of the laws of 1974, constituting the emergency tenant
protection act of nineteen seventy-four, as amended by chapter 403 of
the laws of 1983 increases the period that landlords must produce rental
records from four to six years.

§ 7 corrects a typographical error in subdivision c of section 12 of
section 4 of chapter 576 of the laws of 1974, constituting the emergency
tenant protection act of nineteen seventy-four, as added by chapter 102
of the laws of 1984.

§ 8 adds a new section 5-b to section 4 of chapter 576 of the laws of
1974, constituting the emergency tenant protection act of nineteen
seventy-four that provides that in the event a rental unit had been
moved out of regulation by having a rent overcharge, that unit will
return to regulated status and sets penalties for failure to comply.

§ 9 amends subdivision 3 of section 5 of chapter 274 of the laws of
1946, constituting the emergency housing rent control law, as amended by
chapter 337 of the laws of 1961 to the effect that The Division of Hous-
ing and Community Renewal can revoke an order of eviction even in cases
where there is no finding of fraud or illegality on the part of the
landlord.

§ 10 amends subdivision 5 of section 11 of chapter 274 of the laws of
1946, constituting the emergency housing rent control law, as amended by
chapter 706 of the laws of 1966 to allow a tenant or the Division of
Housing and Community Renewal to file an action for rent overcharges for
a period of up to six years after such a rent overcharge.

§ 11 amends section 213-a of the civil practice law and rules, as
amended by chapter 116 of the laws of 1997 to increase the period for
the commencement of an action in the case of a rent overcharge from a
period of four years to a period of six years after the first over-
charge.

§ 12 sets the enactment date of this act and provisional expiration
dates consistent with other expiration dates of housing and rent control
laws.

 
EXISTING LAW:

Current law provides the authority for a tenant in a rent regulated unit
to look back four years for rent overcharge claims.
In the case where rent overcharges are determined to be the result of
fraud, and in some cases other illegality, a penalty can be assessed
upon the landlord.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

This bill chiefly provides tenants in cases of rental overcharges with
two benefits.

The first is to extend the lookback window for rent overcharges from
four to six years, consistent with the statute of limitation on other
contract actions.

The second is to extend the grounds for imposing a penalty for rent
overcharges, even where there is no fraud or illegality found.  Extend-
ing the lookback window for rent overcharges will allow DHCR to discover
more rent overcharges dating back further in the units rent history, and
to levy penalties based on a longer lookback window.  DHCR will be able
to correct the maximum legal rent resulting from overcharges, regardless
of whether the overcharge is found to be fraudulent or illegal.

This bill also returns units to the rent regulation system if they were
deregulated because of rent overcharges.

 
LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

2017-12: 5.9175

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

None.

 
LOCAL FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

None

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
One hundred and eighty days after passage. Expires in the event of the
expiration of other rent control laws.

summary: Relates to the statute of limitations on rent overcharges; increases from four years to six years; requires records to be kept for six years; requires units to be re-regulated where they have been deregulated due to overcharges.
